title: Undo a commit that is already on main
summary: A bad commit shipped. Reset would rewrite shared history; revert adds a new commit that undoes it. Learn which to use, and how to revert something in the middle of history.
mental_model: `reset` moves a branch pointer — fine for commits nobody has seen. `revert` creates a new commit whose diff is the inverse of an old one — the only honest option once other people have pulled.

steps.title: Find the bad commit
steps.why: The tax rate went from 20% to 2% — a typo that has been live for three commits. It is not the tip, and it has been pushed, which rules out both amend and reset.

steps.title: See why reset is the wrong tool here
steps.why: Reset would move main backwards, discarding the two good commits after it and rewriting history everyone has already pulled. Look at what it would cost before ruling it out.
steps.expect: You and origin are in sync — so any rewrite means a force push.

steps.title: Revert it
steps.why: `git revert <sha>` computes the inverse diff and commits it. History gains a commit rather than losing one, so nobody else has to do anything. The default message names what was reverted.
steps.expect: TAX_RATE back to 0.20, with a new 'Revert...' commit on top.

verify.label: the bad change is undone
verify.hint: git revert <sha of the tax commit>

verify.label: history grew by one commit instead of losing three

steps.title: Confirm the later commits survived
steps.why: Revert only inverts the one commit you named. Shipping costs and the readme are untouched — which is precisely why it is safe to run on a busy branch.

verify.label: commits after the reverted one are unaffected

steps.title: Revert without committing
steps.why: `--no-commit` stages the inverse and stops, so you can revert several commits and land one combined commit, or adjust the result before committing. Handy when the straight inverse is not quite right.
steps.expect: shipping.py staged for deletion, no commit made.

steps.title: Change your mind cleanly
steps.why: `git revert --abort` unwinds an in-progress revert exactly like the merge and rebase equivalents. Every multi-step git operation has this escape hatch.

verify.label: the aborted revert left no trace

steps.title: Push the fix and read the history
steps.why: A normal fast-forward push — no force, no coordination. The history now tells the truth: the change was made, then deliberately undone, and both facts are recorded.

verify.label: the revert reached the server without a force push
the bad tax rate is undone
verify.hint: git revert <sha>, not git reset — the commit was already pushed

verify.label: the good commits that followed it are intact
history grew by a revert commit rather than being rewritten
the server has the revert, pushed as a fast-forward

pitfalls: Reverting a commit does not remove it from history. Anything sensitive in it is still there — revert is not redaction.
If the code has changed since, the inverse diff may conflict. Resolve it like any conflict, then `git revert --continue`.
`git revert HEAD~3` reverts the commit three back, not the last three. For a range, use `git revert <old>..<new>`.
Reverting a revert is a normal thing to do and reads perfectly well in history — `git revert <sha-of-revert>`.
